title: The Future of SAP Is Hybrid: Recent Announcements Support It
summary: Recent announcements from SAP expand integration options for ECC customers, suggesting that an ECC to S/4HANA migration may not be required to modernize ECC.
body_markdown:
On October 29, 2026, at SAP TechEd in Berlin, SAP announced that SAP Business Data Cloud will natively support Apache Iceberg and expand zero-copy data sharing with major data and cloud platforms. The company also stated it will be extending its Databricks partnership to bring data from legacy ERP systems into its cloud analytics platform.


But while the headlines focus on open data formats and cross-platform data sharing, these announcements tell a more interesting story.


SAP is making it easier for data from existing systems, including ECC, to participate in its newer cloud, data and AI architecture. SAP Business Data Cloud is expanding interoperability with Databricks, Snowflake, Microsoft, AWS and Google. The company has even described scenarios in which manufacturers running ECC on-premises bring historical business data into SAP Databricks without first replacing the underlying ERP.\[1\]


This move weakens the simple argument that customers must first replace or migrate their ERP to innovate. It also reinforces the point that customers can modernize around systems that are working, rather than making ERP replacement a prerequisite.


That’s good news for customers. Here’s why.


## The hybrid landscape isn’t going away


Large SAP estates rarely fit neatly into a migration diagram.


A company may run SAP ECC for core finance and manufacturing while implementing S/4HANA elsewhere. SuccessFactors may handle HR, Ariba may take care of procurement and another platform may address customer processes. Microsoft, AWS or Google may support cloud and AI workloads, while data resides across SAP, Databricks, Snowflake and dozens of other systems.


Some of that estate is new, some isn’t and much of it may coexist for years. In fact, the numbers suggest it will.


CIO reports that more than 20,000 SAP customers are still running ECC.\[2\] According to , S/4HANA migration remained customers’ single biggest challenge, with 61% citing budget constraints and 48% struggling with integration.\[3\]


That doesn’t necessarily signal stalled transformation. It may reflect organizations making deliberate decisions about where change creates enough value to justify the cost and risk.


SAP now appears to be designing more explicitly for that reality.


An article in *The Register* highlighted the significance of SAP opening its architecture not only to S/4HANA Cloud but also to ECC users.\[4\]


That matters because it further separates access to data, advanced analytics and AI from the ERP upgrade lifecycle.


## Integration has become part of the strategy


If existing and new systems are going to coexist, integration isn’t something organizations take on temporarily while waiting for a final migration.


It’s part of the architecture.


As such, leaders need to ask:


- *Can the systems exchange data?*
- *Can business processes operate across SAP and non-SAP applications?*
- *Can AI access the information and business context it needs?*
- *Can the environment remain supported and secure?*
- *Can all of it operate at a cost that makes business sense?*


Those questions carry weight, whether the underlying transactional core is ECC, S/4HANA, cloud ERP or some combination of all three.


They also change the conversation around existing ERP systems.


If an ECC instance continues to run critical processes reliably, can be supported and secured, can integrate with modern applications and can make its data accessible to analytics and AI, age alone likely doesn’t make replacement an urgent business priority.


**The stronger question is whether replacing it solves a business problem worth the cost and disruption.**


## Start with the outcome, not the destination


Sometimes a move, including a partial one, can be the right call when the business case supports it. But whether the destination is a newer SAP suite, another vendor’s platform or something else entirely, “move” is a destination decision. It isn’t a modernization strategy.


Increasingly, the ERP core doesn’t have to be the center of every innovation decision. Many architects describe a[“headless” ERP model](https://www.riministreet.com/blog/agentic-ai-erp-the-catalyst-for-enterprise-innovation/) , where the ERP’s data and business logic are exposed through APIs while experiences, analytics, automation and AI are built around the core rather than inside it. This approach complements a broader composable architecture, in which capabilities can be changed or added around a reliable system of record.


In that model, the ERP becomes a stable business core that organizations can modernize and innovate around, as opposed to a platform they must continually replace to gain new capabilities. The question shifts from “Which ERP do we move to?” to “What must change to deliver the desired outcome?”


Modernization should start instead with what the business needs:


- What isn’t working?
- What costs too much?
- Where is risk increasing?
- Which processes need to change?
- Where could automation or AI deliver measurable value?
- Will replacing the ERP solve the actual root cause of the business challenge?


Start there, and a hybrid landscape begins to look less like an unfortunate transition state and more like a deliberate enterprise strategy. Two pressures test that strategy most: the push to adopt AI, and the need to keep what remains in place supported and secure.


## AI makes the distinction harder to ignore


AI is often cited as the reason for replacing on-premises ERP. But even SAP has started to loosen that connection.


At[SAP Sapphire in May 2026](https://www.riministreet.com/blog/post-sap-sapphire-2026-what-executives-should-do-next/) , the vendor said customers running ECC and S/4HANA on-premises could access selected Joule capabilities. Now, the data architecture is opening further. If ECC data can participate in a modern data and AI architecture, innovation doesn’t necessarily have to wait for an ERP migration.


That’s important because many large enterprises already have data and AI investments across Microsoft, Databricks, Snowflake, AWS, Google and other technologies.


AI innovation doesn’t necessarily require a new ERP system; what’s needed is access to the ERP’s data, processes and business context. An API-first, headless approach is one way to expose that information while keeping the transactional core intact.


So instead of asking, “How quickly do we need to move ERP to get AI?”, ask something more practical:


“What business process are we trying to improve, what data does it require and which technology delivers the right outcome at the right cost?”


## Keeping systems supported, secure and connected


A hybrid landscape only works if the systems that remain operational continue to be supported, secured and connected to the applications, data platforms, workflows and AI that the business adopts. This is where the right support and optimization strategy becomes critical. Third-party support, for example, can provide ongoing coverage without tying support to an upgrade cycle, while proactive security approaches can help address evolving risk. Interoperability tools can also help existing ERP work with newer technology without requiring an upgrade solely for compatibility.


Together, these capabilities can help organizations maintain a stable core while connecting it to what comes next. From there, they can optimize processes and make larger changes where the business value justifies them.


Supporting, securing and connecting what you already own through independent services also changes the economics of modernization. Lower support and operating costs can create additional capacity for investments in AI, automation, data, security and better user experiences. And, yes, that may also include ERP migration when the business case supports it.


## Where will the next investment create the most value?


Taken together, SAP’s latest announcements don’t signal a retreat from its cloud strategy. However, they reinforce the reality that, for many large enterprises, the journey from today’s SAP estate to tomorrow’s architecture won’t happen in a single step.


Existing systems and new investments must work together. For example:


- ECC and S/4HANA
- On-premises and cloud
- SAP and non-SAP
- Existing applications and AI


The companies with the strongest SAP roadmaps won’t be the ones that replace existing systems fastest. Instead, they’ll likely be the ones that distinguish between what to keep, what to support and secure, what to connect and improve and what’s genuinely worth replacing.


So instead of asking:


**“When should we retire ECC?”**


Ask:


**“Where will our next investment create the most business value?”**


## Key takeaways


For SAP ECC customers, modernization no longer has to start with the assumption that the ERP core must move. Many enterprises will run a hybrid landscape for years, making support, security and connectivity increasingly important. Greater data and AI can give organizations more flexibility to innovate around existing systems.
